134.title: The scan before sleep
134.hook: many people find a slow scan helps them drift off
134.howItsDone: Many people use a guided body scan or a yoga nidra recording in bed, lying still while attention moves slowly through the body, and some fall asleep before it ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jaw, the shoulders and the belly, where the day gets stored. Your line was let the shoulders down.

It's midnight. The lights are off. Your body is tired, but your head is running a meeting: tomorrow's list, the thing you said at lunch, a song you can't shake. You roll over and check the time, which makes it worse. You tell yourself firmly to go to sleep, which makes it much worse. There's a quieter way in. Instead of arguing with your thoughts, give your attention somewhere slow to go: a trip through your own body, from the toes up, one part at a time.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AND A MEETING IN YOUR HEAD.` → `GO TO SLEEP! (WORSE.)` → `THE SCAN BEFORE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Sleep has a strange rule: it gets harder the more you try. Sleep researchers call it sleep effort. Straining to fall asleep keeps the brain alert, the opposite of what you want. So the scan before sleep doesn't force sleep. It steps out of the way. Two days ago, the body scan was about noticing, wide awake. At night it changes a little. You lie down and move slowly, feet, ankles, calves, knees, and at each place you add one small invitation: this part can rest now. You're not checking whether it does. You give permission, and move on. It works on two fronts. It gives the busy mind a simple, dull job, like counting sheep with more to feel. And it lets yesterday's muscles, the jaw, the shoulders, the belly, finally let go. If you fall asleep before you reach your knees, that's a success. India has a cousin of this with an old name. In the twentieth century, Swami Satyananda Saraswati shaped a practice he called yoga nidra, yogic sleep: lying down, moving awareness around the body part by part. The name reaches much further back. In the Devi Mahatmya, Yoganidra is the sleep, praised there as the goddess, that holds Vishnu on the cosmic ocean between one age of the world and the next. Two different roots, one simple move: a body visited gently, part by part. And if you're still awake at the top of your head, start again at the toes. Nothing is lost.

segments.voice: This is a rehearsal for tonight: lie down if you can, or lean back, and let your eyes close. Starting at the feet, say inside, my feet can rest now, then move up: the legs, the hips, the belly soft, the chest and the breath slow, the hands heavy, the shoulders down, the jaw loose, the eyes. Don't check whether it worked; give each part permission and move on.
Yoga nidra. Yogic sleep: a slow trip through the body at bedtime, giving each part permission to rest instead of forcing sleep. Today's word.
Your line: every part can rest. If you drift off halfway, that's the practice working. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.

135.title: Sleep is practice
135.hook: most adults need roughly seven to nine hours, and no practice replaces it
135.howItsDone: Sleep specialists commonly recommend a regular bedtime and wake time, seven or more hours for most adults, and keeping the same schedule on weekends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yoga nidra, toes to head, each part given permission. Your line was every part can rest.

Here's an honest moment in a course full of practices: breathing, gratitude, walking, the view from above. All good. But if you're sleeping five hours a night, none of it can do what sleep does. You can't breathe your way out of being exhausted, or gratitude-list your way past it. A tired brain is worse at paying attention, which makes it bad at every practice in this camp. So today's practice isn't a technique at all. It's the one underneath the others.
screen: `FIVE HOURS A NIGHT?` → `NO PRACTICE REPLACES IT.` → `SLEEP IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Start with the number. In 2015, two major sleep organizations in the United States reviewed the research and landed in nearly the same place: most adults need seven hours or more, and the usual range given is seven to nine. Some people need a little less, some a little more. Next, the trap. It feels as if you adapt to short sleep. You don't, much. In a 2003 study, people who slept six hours a night for two weeks did as badly on attention tests as people kept awake for a night or two. The striking part: they rated themselves only a little sleepy. Tired people are poor judges of how tired they are. Then the clock inside. Your body runs on a rhythm of about a day, called circadian, from Latin words meaning about a day. That clock likes regular hours. Going to bed and waking at roughly the same time, even on weekends, is one of the simplest things sleep scientists recommend. Much older texts treat sleep as a gift. A Psalm in the Bible says it is vain to rise up early and sit up late, "for so he giveth his beloved sleep." You don't have to share that faith to hear the point: sleep isn't laziness, and it isn't something you earn after enough work. It's the ground every other practice stands on. So this one is simple, and oddly hard. Pick a bedtime. Keep it.

segments.voice: Think of when you need to wake tomorrow, and count back seven and a half hours, plus a little extra to fall asleep: that's your bedtime. Say the time inside, clearly, and picture yourself at that hour tonight, putting things down, lights off. If any part of you argues, one more episode, one more scroll, just notice it.
Circadian. The body's roughly day-long clock, which likes regular hours, the ground every other practice stands on. Today's word.

136.title: The last hour
136.hook: bright screens late tend to push sleep later
136.howItsDone: Sleep specialists often suggest a wind-down hour before bed with lower light, fewer screens and a calm routine, sometimes called sleep hygiene.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the practice underneath every practice. Your line was go to bed.

Before electric light, evenings ended with the sun. It went down. There was firelight, maybe a lamp, then the dark. Then, in a blink, came electric light, then television, then a bright little screen held six inches from your face in bed. Your body's clock is much older than any of that, and it still reads light as a message: it's daytime, stay up. Yesterday was the bedtime. Today is the hour before it, the runway sleep lands on.
screen: `FIRELIGHT, THEN THE DARK.` → `A BRIGHT SCREEN IN BED.` → `THE LAST HOUR.`

segments.voice: As evening comes and light fades, your brain starts releasing melatonin, a hormone that tells the body night has arrived. Bright light, especially the bluish light screens and many bulbs give off, can hold that signal back. In the early two thousands, scientists found special cells in the eye whose main job isn't seeing shapes at all. They measure light and report to the body's clock. Then came a study at Harvard, published in 2015. For five nights, people read on a light-emitting e-reader before bed; for five other nights, a printed book. After the screen, they took longer to fall asleep, their melatonin came later, and they felt less alert the next morning. It was a lab study with a small group, so it's a clue, not a verdict. And light isn't the only thing: a gripping show or a tense group chat wakes the mind up too, whatever the color of the screen. Night mode may help a little; it doesn't make the scroll restful. So the practice here is gentle and old. Let the last hour look a bit more like the old evenings. Lamps instead of overhead lights. Screens off, or at least far away. Something slow in your hands: a book, a cup, a conversation, a stretch. You're not fighting the day. You're dimming it, the way the sky does, a little at a time.

segments.voice: Take your bedtime and count back one hour, then picture that moment: which lights go off, and which lamp stays on? Where does the phone go, charging in another room or face down across this one, and what slow thing will you hold instead? See it clearly, as if it's already evening.
Melatonin, the hormone released as light fades that tells the body night has arrived. Today's word.
Your line: dim the day. Sleep needs a runway to land on. That's day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: Night words everywhere
137.hook: Compline for Christians, the bedtime Shema for Jews, Kirtan Sohila for Sikhs: many traditions close the day with words
137.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Compline or night prayers, many Jews say the bedtime Shema, many Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila, and many Muslims recite the last chapters of the Qur'an before sleep, each in their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: melatonin, lamps low and screens away. Your line was dim the day.

Think of a child being tucked in. There's almost always a little ritual: a story, a song, the same few words every night. Grown-ups tend to drop that. But across the world, whole traditions never did. They close the day with words, in the very last minute before sleep.
screen: `A STORY, A SONG.` → `TUCKED IN WITH WORDS.` → `NIGHT WORDS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Start in a monastery. For centuries, Christian monks and nuns have ended the day with a short service called Compline, from a Latin word for completion. After it, many keep a great silence until morning. Psalm four is sung at Compline in many places, and it holds a line that fits the hour: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep." Now a Jewish home. The Torah says to speak its words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So at bedtime, many Jews say the Shema, Hear, O Israel, with other prayers that ask for a peaceful night. It's called the bedtime Shema, and children often learn it first. Now a gurdwara, or a Sikh family at night. They recite Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, by Guru Nanak, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. It's read at night, when the scripture itself is put to rest for the night, and at funerals: the day closing and the life closing held in the same words. And many Muslims, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recite the last short chapters of the Qur'an before sleep. Each tradition has its own reasons, its own words, its own faith behind them, and each deserves to be understood on its own terms. But notice the shared shape. The day doesn't just stop. It's closed, like a door, with a few words said the same way every night.

Say it inside slowly, as if the lights were already off, and let the week gather behind it: the walk, the scan, the shoulders down, the bedtime, the dim lamp. Then rest in the quiet after the words.
Compline, the Christian service from a Latin word for completion, that closes the day with song and prayer. Today's word.

138.title: One act a week
138.hook: Sikhs call selfless service seva; Jews speak of chesed, Muslims of sadaqa, Christians of charity: different words, each with its own meaning
138.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva at the gurdwara, cooking and serving the free meal called langar, washing dishes or minding shoes, and volunteers of every faith and none keep weekly shifts at food banks and shelters.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Compline and the words many traditions say at night. Your line was the day is done.

In the kitchen of a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, the work is already under way. Someone is rolling out flatbread. Someone is washing a mountain of steel plates. Someone is looking after the shoes by the door. Some of them might be doctors or business owners; you can't tell, and nobody asks. They're serving a free meal to whoever walks in, of any faith or none. Ask what they're doing, and you may hear one word: seva.
screen: `WASHING A MOUNTAIN OF PLATES.` → `WHOEVER WALKS IN IS FED.` → `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Seva means service, and for Sikhs it means selfless service: work done for others with no reward in mind. The Sikh Gurus taught that serving others is part of remembering God, not a break from it, and the free kitchen, the langar, is one of the places it happens. Seva has neighbors, each with its own meaning. Jews speak of chesed, loving-kindness: acts like visiting the sick or comforting mourners, done beyond what's strictly required. Muslims speak of sadaqa, voluntary charity; hadith collected in Sahih al-Bukhari call every good deed a charity, and a kind word a charity too. Christians speak of charity, which in the older English Bible translates the Greek word for love: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Four words. They aren't one word in four languages, and it would flatten each of them to pretend so. What they share is a habit: turning your hands toward someone else, on purpose, over and over. That's where this new week, the one that turns toward other people, lands. Not a single heroic day. A rhythm. One act of service a week, small enough to actually keep. A week gives you time to plan it and room to fit it in, and seven days later, you do it again.

139.title: Help without being seen
139.hook: Maimonides' ladder of giving ranks anonymous giving near the top (Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10)
139.howItsDone: Jews give tzedakah in many forms, and Maimonides counts giving into a trustworthy community fund as close to the secret gift; people of every faith also give anonymously for the same reasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seva and its neighbors, and one small act a week. Your line was one a week.

Be honest: when you do something kind, is a small part of you hoping someone notices? The post about the fundraiser. The casual mention that you helped a friend move. That's human. But it raises a real question: does it matter who sees? In twelfth-century Egypt, a rabbi and doctor named Moses Maimonides wrote a great code of Jewish law, and in it he took giving apart like a watchmaker. He ranked it, rung by rung, from grudging to best. And near the very top sits a gift nobody sees.
screen: `HOPING SOMEONE NOTICES?` → `MAIMONIDES' LADDER.` → `HELP WITHOUT BEING SEEN.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew, the word for this kind of giving is tzedakah, from the root for justice, not just kindness: giving is part of setting things right. In his code, the Mishneh Torah, in the laws of gifts to the poor, Maimonides lays out eight levels. At the bottom: giving grudgingly. A little higher: giving gladly, but less than you should. Higher: giving before you're asked. Then the rungs about who knows. Next, the poor person knows who gave, but the giver doesn't know who received: he tells of sages who tied coins in a cloth behind their backs so the poor could take them unseen. Higher: the giver knows, but the receiver doesn't, like sages who slipped coins through a doorway and left. Near the top, neither knows the other. He recalls a chamber in the ancient Temple where people left gifts in secret and the poor were supported in secret. Why does hiddenness matter so much? It protects the dignity of the person receiving: no one has to look up at you, or feel they owe you. And it keeps the giver from turning kindness into a performance. One rung sits higher still: helping someone stand on their own, with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they never need the gift at all. Jesus says something close in the Gospels: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Two teachers, each in their own world, both pointing at the quiet gift.
screen: `TZEDAKAH: FROM JUSTICE.` · `EIGHT RUNGS OF GIVING.` · `NEITHER KNOWS THE OTHER.` · `DIGNITY FOR THE ONE WHO RECEIVES.` · then, large: `UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: Think of a need you could meet without your name on it: paying for the coffee of the person behind you, an unsigned donation, groceries left on a porch. Picture doing it, and walking away. Notice the small itch to tell someone, let it be there, and let it go unanswered.
Tzedakah, the Hebrew word for this kind of giving, rooted in justice rather than mere kindness. Today's word.
Your line: unseen. A hidden gift guards the dignity of the one who receives it. See you tomorrow.

140.title: Helping helps the helper
140.hook: volunteering is linked to better wellbeing in many studies, though cause and effect are hard to prove
140.howItsDone: Many volunteers describe a warm lift after helping, and wellbeing researchers study it through surveys, experiments with small gifts, and long-term studies of people who volunteer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzedakah, Maimonides' ladder, and the gift nobody sees. Your line was unseen.

A stroller carried up the subway stairs. A hard night sat through with a friend. A Saturday at a food bank. And then the walk home afterward. Volunteers asked about that walk often reach for the same words: better, lighter, sometimes better off than the person they helped. That can feel almost like cheating, as if service should cost something. Researchers have tried to measure it, and they keep finding a pattern, with a catch.
screen: `CARRYING THE STROLLER.` → `WALKING AWAY LIGHTER.` → `HELPING HELPS THE HELPER.`

segments.voice: In the late nineteen eighties, a writer named Allan Luks surveyed thousands of volunteers. Many described the same thing: a warm rush while helping, then a longer calm. He called it the helper's high, and the name stuck. Then the lab got involved. In a 2008 study, researchers handed people envelopes of cash, five or twenty dollars, and told some to spend it on themselves and others to spend it on someone else by evening. The ones who spent it on others were happier at the end of the day, and the amount didn't seem to matter much. Then the long studies. Across many countries, people who volunteer tend to report better wellbeing, and in some studies of older adults, volunteers even lived longer. Now the honest part, the one that's easy to skip. Much of this research finds a link, not a proof. Healthier, happier people may simply be more likely to volunteer in the first place. Untangling cause and effect is hard, and good scientists say so. So nobody can promise that helping will fix your mood. What the evidence allows is modest: for many helpers, helping and feeling better travel together. A proverb in the Bible puts it in farm words: "he that watereth shall be watered also himself." And here's the catch. Help only to feel good, and you start watching yourself instead of the person. The good feeling works best as a surprise, not a goal. So notice it when it comes.
screen: `THE HELPER'S HIGH.` · `FIVE DOLLARS FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `A LINK, NOT A PROOF.` · `A SURPRISE, NOT A GOAL.` · then, large: `IT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring back a time you helped someone, recently or long ago, and replay the moment right after. Where did you feel it, the chest, the face, the shoulders, and was it warmth, relief, tiredness, or nothing much? All of it is information, so just notice, without grading it.
